article_content: CONYERS, Georgia (CNN) -- 'Your daughter is a walking time bomb.' We have heard this more times than I care to remember. Every day, we live in uncertainty, not knowing if her next breath will be her last. After 22 years of darkness, Mandy Young is finally grateful to have a name for her condition. Her illnesses strike swiftly and frequently. It's a daily battle filled with fear, worry, misery, faith, and hope. She has been hospitalized more than 100 times and has endured one life-threatening infection after another. We share her story, our story, hoping to help others. We ensure Mandy knows this is not just her illness; it's our family's journey. She is not alone. It's incredibly challenging to live with a mystery so profound that doctors and scientists named her rare disease after her. This is our story about 'Mandy's Disease.' Mandy was a healthy, nine-pound, green-eyed baby—until the day she was diagnosed with Spinal Meningitis. Hours and days passed slowly, with ICU visits every four hours that felt like torture. 'Your daughter is very sick. Her mind is likely in a vegetative state due to continuous seizures. The stroke has paralyzed the left side of her body,' the doctors said. 'She is in a coma, and we don't think she will wake up. It's time to say goodbye,' they continued. My mind was spinning, my stomach churning, feeling like the wind had been knocked out of me. I whispered, 'No. We won't say goodbye. And neither will you. She has to fight. She has to know we want her to fight.' At 13 months, her left eye turned red. Allergies, Pink Eye, minor infection? All easily treated and cured. By day five, after six trips to doctors and emergency rooms, her eye was swollen shut and looked like raw meat. We finally begged her doctor for more aggressive testing. Surgery, biopsies, and a diagnosis followed: Neisseria meningitidis. Her eye would be replaced with a glass eye—if she lived. At 21 months, Spinal Meningitis struck again. The same dire predictions, ICU stays, seizures, and a raging 106-degree fever. 'She doesn't have the strength to fight another infection of this magnitude. It's time to let go. We're losing her by the minute,' the doctors said. After the first bout of meningitis, we were told, 'No one gets it twice. Enjoy your child!' But it happened again, and then a third time. Doctors suspected an immune deficiency, starting our journey to find answers. Twice a week for the next two years, Mandy underwent blood tests and was isolated. Daily preventative antibiotics were administered, but nothing stopped the infections. A fever blister turned into hundreds during a nap, leading to hospitalization and double pneumonia. Scarlet fever, repeated ear infections, and multiple surgeries followed. An abscess the size of a cantaloupe formed in her abdomen. Immune studies continued, revealing only a low white blood cell count. Years passed with no answers. We traveled the country seeking help. 'Her body is beyond current medical understanding. The test to define her deficiency hasn't been invented yet,' we were told. Then, the predicted time bomb exploded: Gas Gangrene and Clostridium septicemia, a combination not seen since WWII. 'She has a five percent chance to live,' the doctors said. In an attempt to save her life, they amputated her leg and hip. As Mandy lay in a coma, we prayed and intensified our search for a specialist. We found Dr. John Gallin at the National Institutes of Health (NIH). Mandy is now 27. Her immune studies began when she was two, and in May 2003, we received an email: 'We have discovered the basis of Amanda's problem.' Mandy has a genetic defect called IRAK-4, preventing her body from recognizing and fighting infections. She continues to be studied at the NIH in hopes of finding a treatment or cure. Although a cure would be the ultimate gift, knowing the name of her illness is a significant milestone. We searched for 20 years for 'Mandy's Disease,' spending countless weeks and months in hospitals, praying for her survival. Having Dr. Gallin and his team working on her behalf is incredible. Mandy is now pursuing a career in motivational speaking. Of her doctors at the NIH, she says: 'They are like my family too, and I get excited about seeing them. NIH, or 'the house of hope,' is just that—a place for families to find hope, just like we did.'
translated_content: CONYERS, Georgia (CNN) -- 'Teie tütar on käimasolev pomm.' Me oleme seda rohkem kordi kuulnud, kui ma meenutada tahaks. Iga päev elame ebakindluses, mitte teades, kas tema järgmine hingetõus on viimane. Pärast 22 aastat pimedust on Mandy Young lõpuks tänulik, et tal on oma haigusele nimi. Tema haigused löövad kiiresti ja sagedasti. See on igapäevane võitlus, täis hirmu, muret, kannatusi, usku ja lootust. Ta on haiglaravil olnud rohkem kui 100 korda ja on üle elanud ühe eluohtliku infektsiooni teise järel. Me jagame tema lugu, meie lugu, lootes aidata teisi. Me veendume, et Mandy teab, et see ei ole ainult tema haigus; see on meie pere reis. Ta ei ole üksi. On väga raske elada nii suure müsteeriumiga, et arstid ja teadlased on tema harvaesineva haiguse tema järgi nimetanud. See on meie lugu 'Mandy haigusest'. Mandy oli terve, üheksa naela kaaluv, roheliste silmadega beebi—kuni päevani, mil tal diagnoositi selgmeningiit. Tunni ja päevade möödumisel, neli korda tunnis intensiivravioskuse külastused, mis tundusid piinlevad. 'Teie tütar on väga haige. Tema aju on tõenäoliselt komas tõttu pidevatest krampide. Insult on paralüseerinud tema vasaku pool. Ta on komas ja me ei usu, et ta ärkab. On aeg hüvasti jätma', nad jätkasid. Mu peaks keerutama, magu pöörates, tundes, nagu oleks mul hingeäärne löök saanud. Ma viskasin: 'Ei. Me ei ütle hüvasti. Ja teie ka mitte. Tal tuleb võidelda. Tal tuleb teada, et me tahame, et ta võitleks.' Kõigest 13 kuu vanusel tema vasak silm punases. Allergia, konjuktiviit, väike infektsioon? Kõik kergesti ravitavad ja ravitud. Viie päeva jooksul, pärast kuue korda arstide ja kiirabi juures käimist, oli tema silm nii tursetunud, et ta ei näinud midagi ja näis toore liha palana. Lõpuks palusime tema arstil agressiivsemat testi. Operatsioon, biopsiad ja diagnoos järgnesid: Neisseria meningitidis. Tema silm asendatakse klaas silmaga—kui ta ellu jääb. Kõigest 21 kuu vanusel tabas teda taas selgmeningiit. Samad hirmutavad ennustused, intensiivravioskuse viibimised, krambid ja 106-kraadine palavik. 'Tal ei ole jõudu selle suuruse infektsiooni vastu võidelda. On aeg loobuda. Me kaotame teda minutite jooksul', arstid ütlesid. Pärast esimest meningiidi puhangut meile öeldi: 'Keegi ei saa seda kahe korda. Elage oma lapsega ja naudige teda!' Aga see juhtus uuesti ja siis kolmandat korda. Arstid kahtlustasid immuunpuudulikkust, alustades meie teekonda vastuste leidmiseks. Kaks korda nädalas järgmised kaks aastat läbis Mandy vereproove ja eraldati. Igapäevased profülaktilised antibiootikumid manustati, aga midagi ei peatanud infektsioone. Palavikupuhaste muutus sajadeks magamise ajal, mis viis haiglaravile ja topeltkopsupõletiku. Kõrvade põletikud kordusid ja mitu operatsiooni järgnes. Kõhus moodustus kantalupi suurune abstsess. Immuunsüsteemi uuringud jätkusid, paljastades ainult madala valge vereliblede arvu. Aastad möödusid ilma vastusteta. Me rändasime riigi läbi abi otsimas. 'Tema keha on praeguse meditsiini arusaamistest kaugemal. Test tema puuduse määratlemiseks pole veel leiutatud', meile öeldi. Siis plahvatas ennustatud ajaloom, gaasgangreen ja Clostridium septicemia, kombinatsioon, mida ei ole nähtud alates Teisest maailmasõjast. 'Tal on viie protsenti elamise võimalus', arstid ütlesid. Püüdes tema elu päästa, amputeerisid nad tema jala ja püsti. Kui Mandy komas magas, palvetasime ja intensiivsime oma otsingut spetsialisti leidmiseks. Me leidsime dr John Gallini Riiklikus Tervise Instituudis (NIH) Bethesdas Marylandis. Mandy on nüüd 27. Tema immuunsüsteemi uuringud algasid, kui ta oli kaks aastat vana, ja mais 2003 saime e-kirja: 'Lõpuks oleme avastanud Amanda probleemi põhjuse.' Mandyl on geneetiline defekt, mida nimetatakse IRAK-4, mis takistab tema kehal infektsiooni ära tundmist ja selle vastu võitlemist. Teda jätkatakse NIH-s uurimas lootes ravimi või raviviisi leidmiseks. Kuigi ravi oleks ultimaatne kingitus, on tema haiguse nime teadmine oluline samm. Me otsisime 20 aastat 'Mandy haigust', veetes arvutult nädalaid ja kuid haiglatest, paludes tema ellujäämise eest. Dr Gallini ja tema meeskonna töö Mandy eest on suurepärane. Mandy alustab nüüd karjääri motivatsioonikõneles. Oma arstidest NIH-s ütleb ta: 'Nad on nagu minu perekond ja ma olen nende kohtumise pärast rõõmus. NIH, ehk 'lootuse maja', on täpselt see—koht perekondadele lootuse leidmiseks, nagu meilgi.'

article_content: In a recent shocking incident, a British cyclist named Brett Martin stumbled upon the grim aftermath of a brutal murder while on a routine bike ride in the French Alps. Martin, a former Royal Air Force pilot, shared his harrowing experience with BBC News, describing the scene as something straight out of a Hollywood movie. He found three individuals shot dead in a car and another victim lying nearby. This revelation comes as French prosecutor Eric Maillaud and investigating Judge Michel Mollin were in the UK, collaborating with Surrey Police to gather more information. The victims, Saad and Ikbal al-Hilli, were residents of Claygate, Surrey. Authorities are exploring various angles, including Saad's professional life, his connections to Iraq, and a family financial dispute. Martin's detailed account to the BBC offered new insights into the horrific scene that greeted French police near Lake Annecy. He initially thought he had encountered a severe accident involving a cyclist and a car. However, the absence of the cyclist's bike and the car's still-revving engine raised his suspicions. Upon closer inspection, he realized it was a gruesome crime scene. Despite the trauma, Martin acted quickly, putting an injured girl in the recovery position and seeking help. He later retraced his route to aid the investigation. The family of the victims, described as being of Iraqi-Arabic origin, expressed their heartbreak and gratitude for the support from British, French, and Iraqi authorities. The investigation continues, with hopes that the perpetrators will be brought to justice swiftly.

article_content: (CNN) -- When Christie's launches its latest auction at its New York showroom this evening, gavels will fall. Prices, however, will almost certainly rise ... and rise. For its Post-War Masters and Contemporary Evening Sale, one of this year's headline art auctions, Christie's has on offer masterpieces including Francis Bacon's 'Three Studies for a Portrait of John Edwards', Gerhard Richter's 'Abstraktes Bild (712)', and Mark Rothko's 'Untitled' during a night expected to fetch well north of $200 million. Christie's estimates that the Richter work will command a price of between $22 and $28 million, the Rothko between $40 and $60 million, and the Bacon triptych around $80 million. The house has reason to be upbeat with its estimates. On May 12, during an auction titled 'If I Live I'll See You Tuesday', buyers from 26 countries splashed out on contemporary works by artists including Jean-Michel Basquiat, Jeff Koons, and Richard Prince. Christie's sold $134.6 million of art in an hour. Speaking to journalists after the show, Christie's Chief Executive Officer Steven Murphy suggested that buyers from emerging markets are helping keep the market vibrant. 'The number of people around the world interested in acquiring art at all levels is exploding,' he said. 'We are not in a bubble.' Viola Raikhel-Bolot, the director of global art advisory firm 1858 Ltd Art Advisory, believes international buyers will turn out en masse for tonight's auction. 'The place to buy post-war and contemporary art seems to remain New York,' she says. 'Collectors from Latin America and Asia frequent the galleries here and follow these sales very closely.' Read 'The dark side of creativity: Depression + anxiety x madness = genius?' Boom times. In recent years, sales of fine art have trended in one direction: up. According to the annual report of the European Fine Art Fair, global sales of fine art and antiques jumped 7.5% in 2013 to $65.5 billion, just under the all-time high set in 2007. This includes auction sales and estimates of anonymous sales. In 2013, Christie's tallied more than $7 billion in sales, breaking its own record for the fourth consecutive year. In November 2013, a Christie's auction in New York brought in $782,368,375, the highest auction series in art market history. Jeff Koons's 'Balloon Dog (Orange)' sold for $58.4 million, making it the most valuable work sold at auction by a living artist, and at the same auction, Francis Bacon's triptych of Lucian Freud sold for $142 million. Andrew Renton, director of London's Marlborough Contemporary gallery and a professor of curating at Goldsmiths College at the University of London, points out that there are many more deals going on in private, and that some likely outstrip existing records. 'We've got an economic model which is slightly contradictory,' Renton says. 'Prices seem to set the value. Overpaying is almost the best thing you can do, because you start to define your own market.' But this isn't a free-for-all. He believes buyers with deep pockets want superlative works that delve into our psyche. 'Bacon works on that model,' he says. 'He gets into the soul of the anxious human being. And in Rothko, the abstraction is a reflection of the darkness and the contemporary condition.' 'People talk about these things in monetary terms. You don't get to that monetary value unless there is a correlation with cultural value.' As classic works become more scarce, their value will continue to rise -- as will the hoopla surrounding them. 'I do not believe there is a price ceiling,' Renton says. 'In our lifetime we will see a billion-dollar work of art.'

Majal on põhjus olla optimistlik. 12. mail toimunud oksjonil 'If I Live I'll See You Tuesday' ostsid inimesed 26 riigist kaasaegseid teoseid Jean-Michel Basquiat'i, Jeff Koons'i ja Richard Prince'i loomingust ning Christie's müüs tunnis kunsti väärtuses 134,6 miljonit dollari. Oksjoni järel ütles Christie's tegevjuht Steven Murphy ajakirjanikele, et arengumaade ostjad aitavad turu elavana hoida. 'Maailmas on huvitatud inimesi, kes soovivad kunsti omandada kõikidel tasanditel, rohkem ja rohkem,' ütles ta. 'Me ei ole bubilis.' Viola Raikhel-Bolot, globaalset kunstinõustamisfirma 1858 Ltd Art Advisory direktor, usub, et rahvusvahelised ostjad tulevad massiliselt täna õhtul toimuva oksjoni jaoks. 'Postmodernse ja kaasaegse kunsti parim koht osta jääb New York,' ta ütleb. 'Kogujad Lõuna-Ameerikast ja Aasiast sagedamini külastavad siin galeriisid ja jälgivad neid müüke väga täpselt.' Loe artiklit 'Loomingu tumedast küljest: depressioon + ärevus x hullus = geenius?' Õitsengu aeg. Viimastel aastatel on kõrge kunstimüük suundunud ühes suunas: ülespoole. Euroopa kõrge kunsti ja antikvaarse laata aastaraamatu järgi kasvasid 2013. aastal maailmas kõrge kunsti ja antikvaarse müük 7,5 protsenti 65,5 miljardi dollarini, vähem kui rekordiline tase, mis pandi 2007. aastal. See hõlmab oksjone ja anonüümsete müükide hinnanguid. 2013. aastal registreeris Christie's üle 7 miljardi dollari müügi, murdes omaenda rekordi neljandal aastal järjest. 2013. aasta novembris toimunud Christie's oksjon New Yorkis tõi sisse 782 368 375 dollari, kõige kõrgem oksjonisari kunstiturgude ajaloos. Jeff Koons'i 'Balloon Dog (Orange)' müüdi 58,4 miljoni dollari eest, mis teeb sellest elava kunstniku kõige väärtuslikum töö oksjonil, ja samal oksjonil müüdi Francis Bacon'i triptühhon Lucian Freudist 142 miljoni dollari eest. Andrew Renton, Londoni Marlborough Contemporary galerii direktor ja Goldsmiths College'i professor, räägib, et palju rohkem tehinguid toimub privaatselt ja mõned võivad ületada olemasolevad rekordid. 'Meil on majandusmudel, mis on veidi vasturääkiv,' ütleb Renton. 'Hinnad näivad väärtust määrama. Liigne maksmine on peaaegu parim, mida saab teha, sest sa hakkad oma turu ise määrama.' See ei ole aga vaba jooks. Ta usub, et sügavtaskelised ostjad soovivad töid, mis uurivad meie psüüket. 'Bacon töötab sel mudelil,' ta ütleb. 'Ta jõuab ängistunud inimese hinge. Ja Rothko abstraktsioon on tume ja kaasaegse seisukorra peegeldus.' 'Inimesed räägivad neist asjadest rahalistes terminites. Sa ei jõua rahalise väärtuseni, kui ei ole korrelatsiooni kultuurväärtusega.' Klassikaliste tööde vähesus suurendab nende väärtust - nagu ka nende ümberteksti. 'Ma ei usu, et on hinnapiirangut,' ütleb Renton. 'Meie eluajal näeme miljardi dollari väärtust kunstiteost.'

article_content: (CNN) -- Growing up in Utah as a 'crazy kid', what do you do? You strap on your skis and go downhill fast -- very fast. 'I'd say most of the time I'm basically on the verge of crashing,' Ted Ligety -- the 'King of Schladming' and arguably the best male skier in the world right now -- told CNN's Human to Hero series. 'The fastest way down is just being -- one little slip up and you are done -- so that's the fastest way to go down. We're riding a fine line most of the time.' Known as 'Ted Shred' for his fearless attitude on the piste, Ligety's approach to gravity -- traveling at speeds that even motorists might start to feel nervous about -- has served him well since making his pro debut a decade ago. See Ligety's downhill run via headcam. 'For me, I think it's one of the most fun sports out there too because it's such an adrenaline rush -- you're just using gravity,' he said. 'We have courses where you reach speeds of 100 mph (160 kph) so it's very unique in those ways.' Securing a stunning hat-trick of titles at this month's world skiing championships in the Austrian resort of Schladming, the 28-year-old from Park City matched a feat last achieved by the legendary Jean-Claude Killly back in 1968. In doing so, he all but singlehandedly hoisted the United States to the top of the medals table in Austria. Those victories in the super-G, super combined, and his specialty giant slalom, where he was defending his 2011 title, showed Ligety's all-round versatility and catapulted him to superstar status. No-nonsense approach. Not that he is letting his recent success go to his head. The American has even bigger goals ahead -- trying to overhaul Austrian Marcel Hirscher at the top of this season's overall World Cup standings and then challenging for gold at the Sochi 2014 Winter Olympics. 'I still believe the overall (World Cup) title winner is the No. 1 skier in the world,' Ligety said. 'I have been having a great season but I'm a little way back in the overall, so to me Marcel Hirscher is the No. 1 in the world.' 'I had a really hot couple of weeks and luckily that fell during the world championships. I am hopeful I can continue the success of the worlds into the other events besides giant slalom.' Ligety's no-nonsense approach and relentless quest for improvement mean he has swerved the media hullabaloo which accompanies his fellow U.S. teammates such as Lindsey Vonn and Bode Miller. 'I'm not doing ski racing to become famous. I do it because I love it and I'm competitive. That's what drives me. My main focus is on ski racing, not the red carpet,' he states on his official website. Vonn's fall in the women's super-G at Schladming, suffering a serious knee injury, brought her season to a premature end, and with Miller still recovering from a knee injury of his own, Ligety might have to start getting used to a more intensive media glare. Unexpected triumph. Suddenly all the attention is on him, and even he admits that his success was a little unexpected. 'I knew I had very good chances at medals in both the super-G and combined, but to win both was definitely a surprise,' he said. 'My main goal for the worlds was to defend my giant slalom title, so winning the super-G and combined added a little extra pressure.' 'I was so focused on the giant slalom I didn't realize what I had done until it was over. Though it's still hard to fathom that I won three golds and that it has not been done since Killy in 1968.' There is also the smaller matter of Sochi 2014, where Ligety hopes to add to the Olympic gold he won as a 21-year-old in the super combined at the 2006 Winter Olympics in Turin. Ligety insists he is 'not focused on the Olympics yet' but memories of his earlier success leave a warm glow. 'Winning the gold medal in the 2006 Olympics was pretty surreal,' he said. 'I still kind of shake my head when I think about winning the gold medal because I was so young and it was really cool to win the gold. To hear the national anthem and stand on top of the podium was a really surreal experience.' While his career is on an upward trajectory, Ligety downplays suggestions that he will be carrying main U.S. hopes at the Russian resort next February. 'It's far enough away so much can change between now and then. Bode and Lindsey should be healthy for the Olympics so we will have a very strong team besides myself.' Commercial venture. That 2006 victory opened up other commercial opportunities, and Ligety cleverly exploited his nickname to start a similarly-titled company specializing in custom-made helmet and goggle combinations. 'I was a crazy kid and would go straight line moguls and was willing to push myself to another level. And, you know, it rhymes with Ted, so 'Ted Shred' was what I was called.' Ligety may have had a wild streak as a teenager, but he has adopted the same levelheaded approach to business as his skiing career, partnering a friend who brought technical expertise to the venture. 'It's nice to have the distraction of running a company. I wouldn't say I do the day-to-day business side of it just because it would be impossible with my schedule, but it's a fun distraction to take it away from the grind of always traveling and ski racing.' His products are worn by a growing number of fellow World Cup skiers, including Alexis Pinturault, a young Frenchman who beat Ligety into third place as he claimed his maiden World Cup giant slalom win at Garmisch-Partenkirchen last weekend. It was a rare defeat in giant slalom this season for Ligety, who has taken advantage of a change in the length of skis and their turning circle to dominate the discipline. Outspoken critic. Ironically, Ligety was an outspoken critic of the rule changes introduced by world governing body, the FIS, and was perplexed that as a leading competitor he wasn't consulted on the changes. 'I wasn't even talked to about it or asked if I thought it was a good idea, it just happened and I thought it was done in a very improper manner,' he said. He quickly put that lack of consultation to one side when he won an early-season race by more than two and a half seconds -- the margins are usually tenths of seconds -- and Ligety is still waiting for the rest of the world to catch up. The American believes the new regulations play to his strengths as a near 10-year veteran of the circuit and because of his style of starting the turns around the gates a little earlier and finishing a little later. 'It allows me to be cleaner on the edge and accelerate more out of the turns,' he said. Using gravity. As a youngster he was inspired by the exploits of Tommy Moe -- 'my first ski hero' -- who won gold and silver at the 1994 Winter Games in Lillehammer.
